hypothesis: Every mechanism tried so far (feature widening, L2 sweep, UBPR reweighting) has hit the same overfitting signature under plain bilinear FM with only linear+pairwise-interaction capacity — none of them add a genuinely higher-order interaction term, and none has explicit dropout regularization. Swap the scoring function to DeepFM (FM term + an MLP over the same field embeddings, per Guo et al. 2017, present in this project's own model zoo but never wired into the BPR training loop) trained with the same validated BPR pairwise loss, with dropout as an explicit, sweepable regularizer on the added MLP capacity — this should let the model capture non-linear cross-field interactions the plain FM structurally cannot, while dropout controls the overfitting pattern that's plagued every FM variant tried so far.
reflection: The UBPR propensity-reweighting hurt both GAUC and nDCG@5 and overfit even faster than plain BPR (peaked epoch 3, degraded after) — likely because down-weighting popular positives just injected noisier gradients into a linear/bilinear FM that has no spare capacity to absorb them. I'm explicitly skipping the strongly-preferred RESEARCH_QUESTION this turn: the untried categories left (model_architecture, multi_task, data_quality_preprocessing, hyperparameter_capacity, ensembling) are all directly actionable right now from what's already in the provided model zoo and literature notes (DeepFM/AutoInt/xDeepFM code, ESMM description) — there's no missing published-methods knowledge blocking the next step, only an empirical question (does more interaction capacity + explicit dropout regularization help here) that's cheaper to just test directly than to research.
expected_effect: nDCG@5 should move more than GAUC, since higher-order interaction modeling (via the MLP tower) should specifically help distinguish the top few candidates within a user's ranked list beyond what the additive FM linear+bilinear terms can express, while GAUC (global pairwise ranking) is already fairly well captured by the existing FM interaction term.
